translations.text: A confession by Apa Basil, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, which he delivered concerning the end of the age and Solomon’s temple, and concerning departure from the body.
Let us now understand, brothers, that when God was making the whole creation, no one knew.
There was neither sound nor disturbance, but there was great silence and quiet when he made everything.
We have also heard in the holy Scriptures about the day when heaven and earth will be dissolved. Many disturbances are recorded as things that will happen.
For he said that the angels too would work at the dissolution of the world, just as we have heard.
Our Savior told us in the Gospels about the disturbances, afflictions, and earthquakes that will happen.
For he said, “There will be a great affliction, such as has never occurred since the beginning of the creation of the world, and nothing like it [?] will ever happen again.”
He also says in other places, “Heaven and earth will be shaken. The powers of the heavens will tremble on that day.”
There will be great earthquakes, trumpet blasts, and great uproars, crying out with loud voices.
For the angels were spreading out to the four corners of the world,
gathering all humanity together and bringing them to stand before the fearsome judgment seat of the Son of God, separating the ungodly from among the righteous.
Consider, too, the time when he made everything: no one knew except him and his beloved Son, Jesus Christ.
But when he destroys them, the whole creation will be shaken until the final hour and the dissolution of heaven and earth.
No one knew them, not even the angels in heaven, except him and his beloved Son, just as we have already said.
In the days when Solomon built the Lord’s temple in Jerusalem, it was written as follows: “No sound was heard within it, neither an axe nor an iron tool,”
while they were building it for twenty years. The king was building this temple of such magnitude, yet no sound of a craftsman working within it was heard.
Why, then? First, because they were building it for the Lord, in whose dwelling places no disturbance will appear.
Because it was a wise king who was building it for the Lord God, who had chosen Solomon for himself to build him a house of this kind,
in silence, in keeping with the making of the first creation, which he created in silence, without any sound or any disturbance.
For God was working through his own thought and his intention. He has no need of crowds who disturb the place where they work.
God is not like that. Rather, his thought and his command are more than sufficient to produce every kind of craftsmanship.
Therefore, listen to what is written in the Exodus of Moses, when Moses made the tabernacle and the ark of the covenant:
“See,” he said, “that you make everything according to the pattern you were shown on the mountain.”
Who, then, made them, if not the command of God?
This is also how God will build his hidden temple for himself.
This is also what the wise Paul wrote about: “You are the temple of God, and the Spirit of God lives in you.”
And again: “Do you not know that you are the temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you?”
One of the ancient sages also says, “The heart of the wise person is the great altar of God.”
For it was the hand and activity of God that made all creation. It was also this that made humanity.
Listen also to Isaiah speaking in the person of God: “Was it not my hand that laid the foundation of the earth, and my right hand that established heaven?
I will call them all, and they will stand together.”
And again, blessed David cries out: “It was his hands that formed the dry land.”
And again, in Hosea he said: “It was my hand that created the host of heaven.”
And again, in Isaiah: “Heaven is my throne, and the earth is the footstool for my feet.
What house will you build for me?” says the Lord.
“Was it not my hand that made all these things?”
It was also this that formed the first human being, Adam.
For this reason, after the formation of the first human being recorded in Genesis,
the righteous Job also says: “Remember that you formed me from clay, and I will return again to the earth.”
And again: “Did you not pour me out like milk and curdle me like cheese?
You clothed me with skin and flesh, and bound me together with bones and sinews.
You placed life and mercy within me, and your care preserved my spirit.
You have these things in mind. I know that you can do everything, and nothing is impossible for you.”
Then again, David the psalmist says: “It was your hands that formed me and made me.”
And again: “You are the one who brought me out of my mother’s womb.”
And again: “In secret, my bone, which you made in secret, was not hidden from you.”
He also says in Jeremiah: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you, and before you came out of the womb, I sanctified you.”
But after all these things, if it was the hand of God that created all creation—heaven, earth, the sea, and everything in them—
then why would they perish and be dissolved amid great turmoil—creation, humanity, and Solomon’s temple?
And again, the Lord says in the Gospel: “I am working, and my Father is working until now.”
Now the six days that God created, he created with great delight, joy, and gladness.
And he also spent six thousand years providing for the world through his commandments, his laws, and his holy prophets.
And the culmination of all these things: his holy coming to us,
and all the labor of his apostles, and all the provision for human needs, and the course of the heavenly lights.
And yet, after all these things, a single hour will suddenly overturn and destroy the whole creation.
And again, the six days that God spent creating the world—for in the blink of an eye all these things will perish and dissolve.
For it is he, the Lord of everything and the Creator, Jesus Christ, who said in the gospel, “Heaven and earth will pass away.”
And again, “But concerning that day and that hour, no one knows except the Father alone,” because they will not be able to bear the great upheaval that will take place.
Oh, this great anguish! For all the labors of this long time—that is, the administration and service of the angels, the ministry of the heavenly lights,
and the pouring down of rain upon the earth, the blowing of the winds,
the strength that the earth gives to humankind, the flow of the waters of the rivers—
a single hour will wipe all these things away, and they will perish.
How, then, will this single hour be able to bring about all these evils, except through sin and disobedience?
It was the first transgression that threw humanity out of paradise—that is, disobedience.
It changed the world. It caused things that were not meant to happen to happen, and prevented the things that were meant to happen.
It made God, who is free from anger, angry. It made the Father of joy grieve.
Who, then, did all these things? It is sin.
It is everyone's enemy: this evil beast that kills souls, this bird of prey, this biting snake,
the consuming fire, this robber who plunders every soul—sin, this murderous barbarian, this turbulent harbor,
the deserted road, this evil [?]—sin, which summons death and brings mourning,
which stirs up wars, devastates cities, destroys peoples, and makes the whole earth barren.
It is also what causes the rains of heaven to be held back. It also makes parents see their children die and mourn over their loved ones.
It removes kings and leads nations astray, bringing nations into territories that are not their own.
Thorns and thistles came into being because of sin, and because of it death became king. Because of it, too, judgment arose in paradise, and rebukes in the place of delight.
Because of sin, too, weeping came into being in the age to come, and anguish arose throughout the whole creation.
Because of it, the flood came upon the earth, and the floodgates of heaven poured out
their waters of wrath upon the earth. The springs of the deep opened and gushed up waters of vengeance.
Because of it, God considered wiping out the whole creation on the face of the entire earth.
The transgression of the Watchers, who are the giants, brought the flood. Sin, defilement, and the practice of every kind of impurity burned Sodom and Gomorrah.
The meddling of the people of Calneh caused people's languages to change, until they were scattered over the whole earth.
Pharaoh's sin and stubbornness destroyed the people of Egypt.
Lawlessness and idol worship wiped out the seven nations in the land of Canaan.
Sin and disobedience to God killed a million people of Israel in the wilderness,
by sword, fire, and snakes, because they chose sin for themselves and abandoned the Lord their God. Because of all these things,
the Lord cries out through Isaiah: “For look, in my anger I will turn the sea into a desert,
and I will make the rivers a desert. Their fish will dry up because there is no water, and they will die of thirst.
I will cover heaven with darkness and make its covering like sackcloth.”
But sin has done all these things, and because of it this day will be overturned in this single hour,
and all the ordered beauty of this long age, since the foundation of the world, will perish.
Let us also hear about the construction of the great temple that Solomon built in great peace: who was able to demolish it down to its foundations?
For this is what is written in the Third Book of Kingdoms about the temple that Solomon built for the name of the Lord:
“Behold, the God of Israel [?]: no sound of a hammer was heard in it, nor an axe, nor the sound of any iron tool.” For through his great wisdom,
he designated a place a little distance away from the temple, and they did their work there.
He did this so that the noise of the workers would not deafen the king's ears and prevent him from hearing the cases of those who came to him for judgment.
For God had given him peace, with no war anywhere around him,
nor any attack from any direction. Therefore he had no concern except the affairs of the kingdom.
He would rise early every day, go out to the place he had prepared, and sit there,
so that all the work would continue to proceed in order, without any inactivity or neglect.
For this reason he did not allow the craftsmen to work in the place he had established, to prevent the place from remaining noisy and people from failing to hear the king's words.
When he had finished building the house after twenty years, he celebrated the dedication of the house of the Lord.
He went into the temple with all Israel accompanying him. He knelt before the altar of the Lord with his hands stretched out toward heaven.
He prayed like this, saying, “Lord, God of Israel, if heaven and the heaven of heaven cannot contain you, would God really come and live among human beings?
Now then, Lord, listen to the prayer your servant offers to you, so that your eyes and your ears may be open toward this house.”
In short, after his plea, the Lord spoke to him at the altar, saying, “I have heard the prayer you offered to me.
I do not live in houses made by human hands. But because of the labor you have undertaken,
if you keep my commandments and my judgments, which I entrusted to you, my eyes and my ears will be open toward this house you have built.
But if you transgress my commandments, I will cast this great place away from me.
They will tear it down, and it will become a wasteland. Everyone who passes by will be astonished, clap their hands, and mock it, saying, ‘Why have they done these things to this great place?’
And they will say, ‘Because they abandoned the Lord, the God of their ancestors, and served other, foreign gods.’”
See now: after Solomon fell asleep in death, the people sinned and attached themselves to this evil companion, which is sin.
This is also what caused the first human being to sin in paradise, changing the world from the beginning.
It is also what destroyed the temple of the Hebrews through the Chaldeans, whose name is interpreted as “those who scatter” or “those who destroy.”
Solomon spent twenty years building it with precious stones and an extensive workforce, distributed as follows:
eighty thousand burden-bearers; [?] thirty thousand in Lebanon cutting timber; thirty-four hundred overseers; eighty thousand stonecutters in the mountain.
And after all this, this enemy, which is sin, caused them to tear it down in just a few days.
Shall we then say that the Chaldeans spent more than a whole year attacking Jerusalem?
So this single year undid the work of those twenty years because of sin.
What the Hebrews built, the Chaldeans tore down because of people's lawlessness.
What they built in peace, they tore down amid great turmoil.
What Solomon built with wisdom, Zedekiah tore down through his lawlessness.
Rightly, then, did the Lord put this saying into Solomon's mouth for him to speak: “Wise women build houses, but the foolish woman [?] tears it down with her own hands.”
The blessed Paul also says, “Knowledge makes people puffed up, but love builds up.”
All these things happened under Solomon, but the catastrophe of destruction happened under Zedekiah.
The sound of the axes, which were not heard while it was being built by Solomon the wise—
the sound of axes and horses threw Jerusalem into turmoil as they dismantled it through Zedekiah's foolishness.
After this, listen again to Saint Stephen saying, “Solomon built a house.”
But the Most High does not live in something made by human hands. Where, then, will God live? He says, “Will God really live with human beings?”
For this truly happened: our Lord Jesus Christ came from heaven and lived with us, clothed in flesh like ours, except without sin.
This holy and honored temple, which our Savior willingly put on,
is also the one David spoke about when he said, “Your temple is holy and is a wonder in righteousness.”
Truly, the holy Virgin Mary is a real wonder. No human being like her has been born on earth.
Mary, the temple loftier and more honored than Solomon’s, became a home for the true God,
Jesus Christ, Jesus our Lord, through whom glory belongs to the Father, together with him and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.
Of Basil, bishop.
